states.narration: The parentheses name the same whole quantity, x+y, twice. The first term takes three copies of that quantity; the second takes two. We do not need to know x or y to count the copies.
Count the copies together: three plus two. Keep x+y intact. Only the count is being combined; neither x nor y has been added to that count.
There are five copies of the whole quantity. Before opening the parentheses, predict how many contributions of x and how many of y those five copies contain.
Each copy contains both x and y. Five copies therefore contribute five x terms and five y terms. The total value has stayed the same; we have changed what we count together.

editorial.title: Count the whole, then count the parts
editorial.setup: You can add three apples and two apples without knowing what each apple costs. Algebra uses the same idea with a whole expression: count copies of x+y first, then look inside. Here x and y are real numbers; a copy means one contribution to the sum.
editorial.summary: The repeated quantity must really be the same. Compare 3(x+y)+2(x+z): the two parenthesized expressions differ, so this cannot generally become 5(x+y). Other rearrangements are possible, but this particular counting step requires one unchanged group.
